name: CQRS & Event Sourcing
tagline: Separating write-side command invariants from read-side projections while persisting state transitions as an immutable append-only event log.
purpose: Build a progressive mental model of CQRS and Event Sourcing—from aggregate hydration and optimistic concurrency to read-your-own-writes watermarks and crypto-shredding.

spark.summary: CQRS separates write-side command validation from read-side query projections, while Event Sourcing persists every state transition as an immutable append-only log of domain events rather than overwriting current rows.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use CQRS without Event Sourcing whenever read and write shapes diverge; adopt Event Sourcing only when an immutable audit log, temporal replay, or multi-projection architecture justifies handling eventual consistency and schema evolution.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** **CQRS** (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) splits an application's data model into two paths: a **Command** side that validates business invariants and mutates state, and a **Query** side that reads pre-shaped, denormalized views.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Event-Sourced Command Path & Asynchronous Read Projections (Command Handler -> Append-Only Event Log -> Postgres Read View -> Elasticsearch / OLAP); Optimistic Concurrency & Stream-Version Watermark (Client -> Command Agg -> Event Store -> Read Projection); Event-Sourced Command & Projection State Machine (HYDRATING -> APPENDED -> CONFLICT).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Pick the simplest architecture that satisfies your audit, scaling, and consistency requirements. Never dual-write to Postgres and Kafka in separate calls—use a dedicated Event Store or the Transactional Outbox with Debezium CDC.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore how Transactional Outbox CDC, dual-write drift elimination, read-your-own-writes consistency, and event schema evolution support CQRS in production.

learningJourney.title: What are CQRS & Event Sourcing
learningJourney.explanation:
**CQRS** (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) splits an application's data model into two paths: a **Command** side that validates business invariants and mutates state, and a **Query** side that reads pre-shaped, denormalized views.

**Event Sourcing** changes *how* the Command side persists state. Instead of executing `UPDATE accounts SET balance = 150`, it appends immutable domain events (`FundsReserved`, `TransferSettled`) to an append-only log. Current state is the left-fold (`reduce`) of all events in that stream.

sectionDiagram.title: Event-Sourced Command Path & Asynchronous Read Projections
sectionDiagram.summary: The append-only event log is the single source of truth; read projections tail it asynchronously without locking the write path.

learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how CQRS & Event Sourcing works from first principles.

learningJourney.title: Why we need CQRS & Event Sourcing (and Stale-Read Watermarks)
learningJourney.explanation: Traditional CRUD forces one normalized schema to serve both transactional invariant checks and complex reporting/search queries, causing lock contention and N+1 joins. However, decoupling write and read stores introduces **projection lag (10–200 ms)**: returning `streamPosition` in the command response lets clients wait or fall back until the projection catches up.

sectionDiagram.title: Optimistic Concurrency & Stream-Version Watermark
sectionDiagram.summary: Passing streamPosition=42 from command response to query read prevents stale UI flashes during async projection lag.

learningJourney.title: Where CQRS & Event Sourcing Fit (and Where CRUD Wins)
learningJourney.explanation: CQRS and Event Sourcing are orthogonal: you can use CQRS over a plain relational DB without Event Sourcing, and reserve Event Sourcing for domains that genuinely need an immutable audit log or temporal replay.

benefits: Structurally immutable audit trail of every state transition and business intent.
costs: Requires event schema upcasters and crypto-shredding for GDPR erasure.

benefits: Write store stays append-only; read models use specialized Redis/Elasticsearch shapes.
costs: Eventual consistency lag requires client-side `streamVersion` watermarks.

benefits: Overwriting rows in PostgreSQL is far simpler and gives immediate strong consistency.
costs: Event Sourcing adds unnecessary replay, snapshot, and upcasting complexity.

learningJourney.title: How to manage Snapshots, Idempotent Projections & Upcasters
learningJourney.explanation:
1. **Optimistic Concurrency**: Append events with `expectedVersion` so concurrent writers cannot overwrite invariants.
2. **Periodic Snapshots**: Snapshot aggregate state every 100–500 events so hydration latency stays bounded.
3. **Idempotent Projections**: Store `(streamId, eventNumber)` in the same transaction as the read-model update to survive at-least-once replay.
4. **GDPR Crypto-Shredding**: Encrypt PII inside immutable events with a per-user KMS key; delete the key on erasure request.

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: CRUD vs. CQRS-Only vs. Full Event Sourcing
learningJourney.explanation: Pick the simplest architecture that satisfies your audit, scaling, and consistency requirements.

benefits: Zero projection lag; trivial schema migrations; minimal operational overhead.
costs: Read/write lock contention under heavy analytics/search; loses state history.

benefits: Independent read stores (Elasticsearch/Redis) without immutable event-stream lock-in.
costs: Eventual consistency on reads; no built-in temporal state replay.

benefits: Full temporal replay, auditability, and ability to spawn new read projections retroactively.
costs: Requires upcasters for schema evolution, snapshots, and idempotent projection handlers.

learningJourney.purpose: The trade-off: compare competing approaches across latency, consistency, and operational cost.

learningJourney.title: Production Architecture: Aggregate & Projection Lifecycle
learningJourney.explanation: Never dual-write to Postgres and Kafka in separate calls—use a dedicated Event Store or the Transactional Outbox with Debezium CDC. Keep projection handlers strictly deterministic (no `time.Now()` or external HTTP calls during replay).

knowledgeCheck.question: A user submits a command that updates their account balance and immediately refreshes the page, seeing their old balance because the async read projection is 120 ms behind. What is the cleanest fix?

options.text: Block the HTTP command response until all 5 downstream projections finish updating
options.feedback: Blocking on all projections couples write availability and latency to every downstream consumer.

options.text: Return the committed `streamPosition` in the command response and have the read query wait briefly or fall back until the projection reaches that checkpoint
options.feedback: Correct: passing a `streamPosition` watermark gives read-your-own-writes consistency without stalling all writes.

options.text: Disable optimistic concurrency (`expectedVersion`) on the event store
options.feedback: Disabling `expectedVersion` causes lost updates and corrupted aggregate invariants.
